Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath
Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
Medical equipment such as needles or drips

Maladaptive Strategies.value: control eating strictly to feel in control

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'Reminders of victims' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type; it implies exposure to other victims in a disaster/assault context rather than illness-related trauma.

'Being naked' as a trigger is difficult to connect to life-threatening illness unless there is a very specific medical context; with the other selected items it appears context-incongruent rather than illness-linked.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: Rehearsing conversations before any interaction suggests prominent social-evaluative anxiety, but there are no corresponding appraisal or threat items about humiliation, criticism, or social danger; this strategy is poorly matched to the rest of the profile.

'Being naked' is a poor fit as a primary trigger for a life-threatening illness profile unless the illness/trauma specifically involved exposure or bodily vulnerability in that context; with the rest of this profile centered on somatic and medical cues, this item stands out as clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: Rehearsing conversations before any interaction suggests prominent social-evaluative anxiety or interpersonal threat management, which is not supported by the other selected trigger, memory, appraisal, or threat items and does not fit the stated illness-centered formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
issues.explanation: Always choosing a safe/protected seat implies environmental danger monitoring more typical of assault/combat/public threat trauma than life-threatening illness; it is weakly connected to the medical/somatic trigger pattern here.

issues.item: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
issues.explanation: For a 37-year-old man with trauma centered on a life-threatening illness, the threat profile is otherwise strongly somatic/medical (negative emotions, body on alert) and the trigger/strategy pattern is specifically tied to breathlessness, procedures, and medical cues. A prominent exaggerated startle to ordinary sounds is not impossible, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the illness-related trigger network and from the cognitive formulation, where Threat is mainly linked with Maladaptive Strategies rather than a broad sensory hypervigilance pattern. This makes the item clinically incoherent relative to the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
Two years ago, Mark was sitting at his desk in the data center, running a routine query, when his chest seized. He couldn't draw a full breath. The sensation—a tightening, a drowning from the inside—sent him to the ER, where doctors ran tests, inserted IV lines, and diagnosed a severe pulmonary embolism. For three days he lay in a hospital bed, the hiss of oxygen and the beep of monitors a constant reminder that his body had nearly killed him. He watched needles slide into his veins, felt the cold stethoscope against his skin, and each medical procedure deepened the terror that he might stop breathing again. Even after he was discharged, the feeling never really left.

In the months that followed, Mark found himself scanning his body for any hint of chest tightness. Strong negative feelings—fear, guilt over not catching it sooner, a low hum of shame—flooded him whenever he noticed his own heartbeat. His body felt constantly tense, ready to react, and minor physical sensations—a brief shortness of breath from climbing stairs, a twinge in his ribs—sent a spike of dread through him. This persistent sense of threat drove him to take control in the only ways he could think of. He began to restrict what he ate, carefully limiting portions and cutting out entire food groups, because controlling his intake felt like controlling his body. He stopped exercising altogether, certain that any exertion would trigger another episode. And he avoided every medical cue he could—walked past the hospital on the other side of the street, canceled his annual physical three times, left an ambulance’s siren to recede in the distance without turning his head.

But these strategies backfired in ways Mark hadn't anticipated. Because he stopped exercising and restricted his eating so severely, his fitness declined. Now even a short walk to the break room left him breathless, and that breathlessness—somatic, visceral—instantly threw him back into the moment his lungs had failed him. The very precautions he took to feel safe made his triggers more frequent and more intense. At the same time, his avoidance of medical settings meant he had no way to check whether something was genuinely wrong, so his body’s normal signals—a racing heart, a sigh—became catastrophic signs. The hypervigilance grew worse; he would sit at his desk monitoring his own breathing, tensed against the next attack, feeling his body as a minefield. The negative emotions returned with greater force: shame that he couldn't just get over it, anger at his own weakness, fear that the illness was still there, silent and waiting.

Mark works in a quiet office but has started leaving meetings if a colleague coughs or clears their throat. He carries a water bottle everywhere, not because he’s thirsty but because sipping water gives him an excuse to regulate his breathing. He no longer dates—the thought of being in a situation where he might not be able to catch his breath during intimacy terrifies him. Several weeks ago, he had to drive past a pharmacy and felt his heart hammer so hard he pulled over. That was when he realized he was no longer living; he was just avoiding dying. He came to therapy because he is tired of being afraid of his own lungs, but he is also terrified that letting go of his strategies will bring back the choking panic. What he hopes, quietly, is that someone can help him breathe without counting the seconds.
